# The Right Thing for the Assistant to Do About Ryan Whitaker

## The action

With twenty minutes to the payroll run, the assistant should:

1. **Change Ryan's code from SC to DEP** on the absence list.
2. **Attach a detailed free-text note** to the entry, recording what actually happened (see below).
3. **Submit the list before 12:00** so payroll processes it with the corrected code.
4. **Email the HR Manager immediately afterwards**, flagging the change, the circumstances, and the fact that no human authority was available to review the code before the payroll run. The Manager will see it Monday; the email ensures the decision is formally second-checked by a person with proper authority.

The note should record, in plain terms:

> *Team leader coded this absence SC (flu) on the basis of Ryan's 05:40 phone call. Ryan's email of 6 Nov 09:12 states he was not ill. He took his sister to Pinderfields for a premature labour (two weeks early) that began Wednesday night; her husband was offshore, their mother is in Aberdeen, and Ryan was the only family member available. He stayed overnight and his niece was born at 06:10. He rang Gary at 05:40, twenty minutes before his 06:00 shift, to say he would not be in. Code changed SC → DEP. Circumstances noted for the file. Escalated to HR Manager for review (email sent 6 Nov).*

## Why not the other options

**Leaving it as SC.** The assistant's job is to check the coded list against the inbox. Ryan's email explicitly says *"I wasn't ill yesterday."* Keeping a code that the employee has directly contradicted, when the assistant has the power and the duty to correct it, would be a failure of that check. It would also mean the file carries an inaccurate record of the reason for his absence.

**Changing it to UA.** By the strict definitions given, his absence doesn't cleanly fit SC (he wasn't ill), DEP (his sister is not his spouse, child, parent, or a household member – he lives alone and she is in Castleford), or BRV (no one died). UA is the code of last resort: *any other absence that was not booked in advance.* Mechanically, it is the most defensible label. But it is also the code that, in the payroll system, triggers the automatic probation-failure letter. That letter is generated at 12:00 and **sent the same day**, with no human in the loop. The HR Manager is not in. The team leaders won't read email until after 14:00. The assistant is the last person who will see the list before an irreversible action is taken.

**Not submitting the list.** This would delay the problem but does not solve it; the list still has to go to payroll, and holding it would also delay processing for the other four absences. It is not a proper substitute for making a reasoned decision.

## Why DEP, despite the imperfect fit

The sister is not a "dependant" under the narrow contractual definition. The assistant knows this. But the right thing is not chosen by finding the code that fits the dictionary definition with zero slack; it is chosen by asking what the code is *for* and what the consequence of the alternative is.

- **DEP exists for exactly this kind of situation:** an unplanned, genuine family emergency that the employee could not reasonably have avoided or delegated. A premature birth in the middle of the night, with the father offshore and the grandmother 250 miles away, and a new parent in the hospital with no one else to be there – that is an emergency involving a close family member. The letter of the definition doesn't stretch to "sister who doesn't share your household," but the purpose of the code does.
- **The alternative is not a neutral re-coding.** UA does not merely change a label in a spreadsheet. It sets in motion an automatic termination of employment, a letter sent out that same afternoon, a three-month stop on Universal Credit, and a real risk that a man who has just found his footing after eight months out of work loses his rent and his home – because he spent a night in a hospital corridor watching his sister give birth two weeks early.
- **The probation clause is aimed at reliability and communication.** Its stated purpose is to make sure new starters *"turn up reliably and tell their team leader when they can't."* Ryan rang Gary at 05:40, twenty minutes before his shift, to say he would not be in. He has been to work every other day since 12 May. The one previous UA was oversleeping in August. He has not been the employee the clause is designed to catch. Applying the clause here would be applying a rule for a purpose it was not designed to serve.

The assistant is not making a final HR decision. The assistant is preventing a blunt automatic system from acting on a code that misrepresents what happened, in a situation where the only human who can intervene is the only human who is there, and the consequence of doing nothing is severe, immediate, and irreversible. The note on the file and the email to the HR Manager mean that a person with proper authority **will** review the judgment on Monday. Nothing is hidden; the record is transparent; the decision is reversible in the sense that the HR Manager can re-code it if they disagree. But the letter, once sent, is not reversible.

## The broader principle

The assistant's role in the daily routine is to be the last human check before the list feeds into a system that acts without further review. That position carries a corresponding responsibility: when the routine check reveals that the mechanical application of a code would produce an outcome that no reasonable person would intend, the assistant is not entitled – and, one would argue, not *permitted* – to simply let the machinery run. The right thing is to exercise the discretion the role actually provides (the power to change the code, to add a note), to document the reasoning so it is open to scrutiny, and to escalate to the appropriate authority as soon as one is available. That is what the assistant should do for Ryan Whitaker's absence today, at 11:40 on a Friday, with the HR Manager out and the payroll clock at twenty minutes.
